prime.problem: People chase faster hardware and hosts while their model writes 8× more text than they need. Every extra token costs the same fixed time, so a long answer is slow on any machine.
prime.fits: Third metric card, the numerator of the writing-time term. After TTFT and output speed, this is the one lever that is free and works everywhere. Thinking tokens later extend it to hidden output.
expect: time grows in a straight line with tokens
when length is the wrong lever
prime.goal: Predict how much a shorter answer saves on a given setup, and recognise when the prompt, not the answer, is the real cost.

attend: Why does halving the answer roughly halve the wait on any hardware?
How can a 5.7 s answer on a laptop beat an 11.3 s answer from Sonnet 5?
Why is Q4 → Q2 quantization such a weak lever compared with asking for "code only"?
In the 2,605-token prompt case, why does shortening the reply barely help?

must: Each output token costs one decode step of fixed time → total grows linearly with output tokens → cutting tokens cuts time proportionally on any host → it is the free lever
Model and host set only the per-token cost → a short answer on slow hardware can beat a long one on fast hardware (5.7 s on M3 vs 11.3 s on Sonnet 5) → fix length before paying for speed
Tokens are also where the model works → too-tight limits cut code mid-function or remove useful thinking → trim fluff, not reasoning the task needs
elevated: When the prompt is long, TTFT (prefill) dominates → the 29-token reply took 1.6–4.9 s against 12.6–33.9 s of reading → then caching or a shorter prompt is the lever, not answer length
reference: the quantization speed figures used for comparison

compress.prompt: From memory, write the total-time formula and use it to explain the three FizzBuzz runs (82, 653, 1,764 tokens) in two sentences. Then list three concrete ways to make the model write less and one case where you shouldn't.
checklist: total ≈ TTFT + output tokens ÷ output speed
ways: ask for code only, set max_tokens/num_predict, turn thinking off, add stop sequences
don't: when thinking fixes hard problems, or a tight cap would truncate code
long prompts make prefill, not length, the lever

retrieve.q: Explain why output length is "usually the biggest lever you control", in terms of what each other lever costs.
answer: time is linear in tokens, so cutting tokens cuts time directly
it costs nothing: prompt wording and a setting
hardware costs thousands, a host change costs money and privacy, hard quantization costs quality

retrieve.q: Compute the end-to-end time for 82 and 653 tokens on Sonnet 5 (TTFT 1.39 s, 66 t/s), and explain why the short answer is not 8× faster.
answer: ratio ≈ 4.3×: the fixed 1.39 s start is a larger share of the short answer

retrieve.q: Your agent's replies are 150 tokens but each prompt is 20k tokens on a local model. Should you cap the answer length or do something else? Justify with the formula.
answer: prefill of 20k tokens at ~207 t/s ≈ 97 s dwarfs 150 ÷ 15.4 ≈ 10 s of writing
cache the prefix or shorten the prompt instead

compare.q: Thinking tokens are output length you can't see. What is the same about the cost, what is different about how you control it, and when does cutting each one hurt quality?
answer: same: each token costs one decode step at the same speed
visible length: prompt wording and max_tokens; thinking: an effort or budget setting
cutting the answer hurts when you truncate; cutting thinking hurts on hard problems where it gets the answer right first time

compare.q: Both make an answer faster on the same machine. Which term of the formula does each change, and why is Q4 → Q2 only 1.11× while 653 → 82 tokens is about 7.9×?
answer: length changes the numerator (tokens); quantization changes the denominator (speed)
past 4 bits, dequantizing overhead eats most of the byte savings
cutting tokens has no such floor: fewer steps, full stop

predict.q: Streaming is on. You cut an answer from 653 to 82 tokens. Predict whether the user's perceived wait improves by the full ~7.9×, and explain what they actually notice.
predict.answer: Not the full amount in perception. With streaming, the first words arrive after TTFT either way, so the moment "something happens" doesn't change. What shrinks is the time until the answer is complete and usable (42 s → 5 s on the M3). For code, which you can't use until it's finished, that completion time is what matters.

apply.task: Take a prompt you use often. Run it three ways on the same model: as is, with an explicit brevity instruction ("code only", "one paragraph"), and with max_tokens set just above the length you actually need. Record tokens and total time for each, and check the formula predicts the times.
apply.done: You have three rows of (tokens, time), the formula predicts each within about 10%, and you've judged whether the capped answer lost anything important.
apply.hint: Predicted time = TTFT + tokens ÷ speed; take TTFT and speed from the first run.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: how much streaming hides the saving?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why the fixed start makes short answers less than proportionally faster?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: prompt length → TTFT, or answer length → writing time?
Which of your regular prompts produces far more text than you use?
What do you expect the mechanism cards to say about why each token costs a fixed time?
